meta.description: Yes — it's genuine Aristotle, from the Nicomachean Ethics (Book I). The popular line lightly smooths W. D. Ross's 1925 translation of the Greek.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 384–322 BC · Greek philosopher, Plato’s pupil & Alexander the Great’s tutor
answer.sourceLine: This is genuine Aristotle — the defining formula of his ‘Nicomachean Ethics’ (Book I). W. D. Ross’s standard 1925 translation renders it “human good turns out to be activity of soul in accordance with virtue” (1098a16) and “happiness is an activity of soul in accordance with perfect virtue” (1102a5). The popular one-liner smooths this to “the soul” and drops “perfect,” but the thought and wording are unmistakably Aristotle’s.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Human good turns out to be activity of soul in accordance with virtue, and if there are more than one virtue, in accordance with the best and most complete. … Since happiness is an activity of soul in accordance with perfect virtue, we must consider the nature of virtue.
trail: The core definition sits at Bekker 1098a16 in the Ross translation on Wikisource: “human good turns out to be activity of soul in accordance with virtue.”
Aristotle restates it at 1102a5 as “happiness is an activity of soul in accordance with perfect virtue” — also in the Internet Classics Archive (Ross).
Wikiquote’s sourced entry credits the wording to W. D. Ross and cites Book I, 1098a.
source.excerptNote: W. D. Ross translation (1098a16 and 1102a5). Note Ross writes “of soul” without the article and “perfect virtue” at 1102a — the widely shared “of the soul … in accordance with virtue” is a light modern smoothing.

source.rightsNote: Aristotle’s Greek has been public domain for over two millennia. The exact English wording here tracks W. D. Ross’s translation, first published in 1925 (The Works of Aristotle Translated into English, Vol. IX, Oxford: Clarendon Press) — also public domain in the United States as a work published before 1931. Modern in-copyright translations (e.g. Irwin, Crisp, Bartlett & Collins) phrase the line differently.

author.heading: About Aristotle
author.metaLine: 384–322 BC · Greek philosopher · founder of the Lyceum
author.bio: Aristotle of Stagira was a student of Plato and tutor to Alexander the Great. His Nicomachean Ethics argues that the highest human good is eudaimonia — flourishing achieved through the active, lifelong exercise of virtue rather than as a passive feeling.

misattribution.heading: Wording note
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Aristotle is correct — the only wrinkle is the wording, which circulates in a lightly polished form.

items.why: Ross’s standard text reads “activity of soul in accordance with virtue” (no article) and, at 1102a, “in accordance with perfect virtue.” The meme form inserts “the” and drops “perfect,” per the Wikisource Ross text.

Aristotle’s Greek word is eudaimonia, closer to “flourishing” or “living well” than momentary happiness — a nuance the one-line quote necessarily flattens, as discussed in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Aristotle: the line is his definition of the human good in Nicomachean Ethics, Book I (1098a) — just tidied a touch in popular quotation.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: In Book I of the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle asks what the ultimate goal of human life is — the thing pursued for its own sake and not for the sake of anything else. His answer is eudaimonia, and his celebrated “function argument” concludes that if a human being’s characteristic activity is reasoned activity of the soul, then the human good is that activity performed well — that is, in accordance with virtue.

This reframed happiness from a feeling or stroke of luck into something you do: a lifelong practice of acting excellently. It is the foundation of virtue ethics and still anchors modern debates about well-being and flourishing.
context.pull: Not a mood you fall into, but an activity you practise well — over a whole life.
